Next-item ranks on prefixes whose targets contributed to training are in-sample diagnostics. Strong ranks can reflect memorized transitions, popularity, or transferable sequence structure; freezing the model does not remove this ambiguity. Likewise, a rank drop after shuffling demonstrates sensitivity to order on those examples, not future predictive value. “Does It Look Sequential?” evaluates frozen models on shuffled held-out histories and measures accuracy degradation and top-K overlap; applying its approach to training prefixes supports a narrower interpretation. [Klenitskiy et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008v1)

Recommended training-only protocol: exclude the target and subsequent interactions from each input; preserve left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Compare original prefixes with repeated permutations, permutations preserving the last item, and recent-history truncations, keeping targets and candidate sets identical within comparisons. Report paired target-rank changes and top-K overlap, uncertainty across users, and results stratified by prefix length, target popularity, and transition frequency. These are proposed controls: they help separate recent-item dependence from broader order sensitivity, but cannot distinguish memorization from generalization conclusively. Perturbations can also create unfamiliar inputs, so degradation alone is insufficient evidence of useful temporal reasoning.

Keep all official splits and validation scoring unchanged; label these measurements explicitly as training diagnostics. Establishing temporal generalization requires predictions on interactions excluded from fitting. Research shows that ignoring the global timeline can alter accuracy and model rankings, and that split design materially affects sequential-recommendation conclusions. Here, those findings limit interpretation rather than authorize replacing the benchmark: select models using the prescribed macro validation HR@10, without claiming deployment-time temporal validity from training-prefix probes. [Ji et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060), [Gusak et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16289)
